title: Ὁδοιπόροι καὶ πέλεκυς
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 256. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.l: Two men were travelling in the same place.
sentences.i: Two men were on the road together.
sentences.n: ταὐτῷ is τῷ αὐτῷ run together by crasis, and ἐν ταὐτῷ, 'in the same place', is the phrase used at fable 39 of the fox and the monkey, at fable 246 of two men at the same counter, and again at fables 272 and 276 of this batch. ὡδοιπόρουν is the imperfect of ὁδοιπορέω, the augment lengthening the opening ὁ to ὡ.

sentences.t: Ἑτέρου δὲ πέλεκυν εὑρόντος, ὁ ἕτερος ἔλεγεν· « Εὑρήκαμεν. »
sentences.tr: Heterou de pelekyn heurontos, ho heteros elegen· « Heurēkamen. »
sentences.l: And the one of them having found an axe, the other said: « We have found it. »
sentences.n: The whole fable turns on the person of one verb: εὑρήκαμεν is 'we have found', εὕρηκας 'you have found'. The finder is the first ἕτερος; it is the other who claims a share by saying 'we'.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἕτερος παρῄνει μὴ λέγειν « Εὑρήκαμεν, » ἀλλ’ « Εὕρηκας. »
sentences.tr: Ho de heteros parēinei mē legein « Heurēkamen, » all’ « Heurēkas. »
sentences.l: But the other urged him not to say « We have found it », but « You have found it ».
sentences.n: ὁ δὲ ἕτερος here is the finder, correcting the man who had just claimed a share: Greek uses ἕτερος of either of a pair, so the same word points now at the one man and now at the other. παραινέω takes the dative of the person advised and an infinitive of what he is to do; the negative with such an infinitive is μή, not οὐ.

sentences.t: Μετὰ μικρὸν δὲ ἐπελθόντων αὐτοῖς τῶν ἀποβεβληκότων τὸν πέλεκυν, ὁ ἔχων αὐτὸν διωκόμενος ἔλεγε πρὸς τὸν συνοδοιπόρον· « Ἀπολώλαμεν. »
sentences.tr: Meta mikron de epelthontōn autois tōn apobeblēkotōn ton pelekyn, ho echōn auton diōkomenos elege pros ton synodoiporon· « Apolōlamen. »
sentences.l: And a little afterwards, those who had lost the axe having come upon them, the one who had it, being pursued, said to his fellow-traveller: « We are undone. »
sentences.i: A little later the men who had lost the axe came upon them, and the one who had it, with them on his heels, said to his fellow-traveller: « We are done for. »
sentences.n: ἀποβάλλω is 'to throw away' and hence 'to lose'; the perfect participle names the men by the state they are in — the men who are out an axe. ἀπολώλαμεν is the intransitive perfect of ἀπόλλυμι with present force, 'we are ruined', the same form as the sick man's ἀπόλωλα at fable 249.

sentences.t: Ἐκεῖνος δὲ ἔφη· « ⟨Μὴ ἀπολώλαμεν εἴπῃς⟩, ἀλλ’ ἀπολώλα· οὐδὲ γάρ, ὅτε τὸν πέλεκυν εὗρες, ἐμοὶ αὐτὸν ἀνεκοινώσω. »
sentences.tr: Ekeinos de ephē· « ⟨Mē apolōlamen eipēis⟩, all’ apolōla· oude gar, hote ton pelekyn heures, emoi auton anekoinōsō. »
sentences.l: But that man said: « ⟨Do not say 'we are undone'⟩, but 'I am undone'; for you did not, when you found the axe, make me a partner in it either. »
sentences.i: But the other said: « Do not say 'we are done for', but 'I am done for'; for when you found the axe you did not make me a partner in it either. »
sentences.n: μή with the aorist subjunctive (εἴπῃς) is the regular Greek prohibition against a single act, 'don't say it'. ⟨Μὴ ἀπολώλαμεν εἴπῃς⟩ is Chambry's own supplement, his angle brackets marking words he adds to fill the sense. ἀνακοινόομαι in the middle is to make another a sharer in a thing. The page prints ἀπολώλα where the ordinary Attic first person singular is ἀπόλωλα; the reading is left as printed.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι οἱ μὴ μεταλαβόντες τῶν εὐτυχημάτων οὐδὲ ἐν ταῖς συμφοραῖς βέβαιοί εἰσι φίλοι.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti hoi mē metalabontes tōn eutychēmatōn oude en tais symphorais bebaioi eisi philoi.
sentences.l: The story shows that those who have had no share in the good fortunes are not steadfast friends in the misfortunes either.
sentences.n: μεταλαμβάνω takes the genitive of what one gets a share of. βέβαιος is what stands firm and will not give way — of a friend, one who holds.
